explanations.explanation: Saul, Israel's king, did the opposite of staying home. After the Ziphites, people from around Ziph, told him where David was, he went down to the Wilderness of Ziph with three thousand chosen men of Israel to search for David (1 Samuel 26:2). The tip was one sentence long, and the king was packed and marching. I wish my own to-do list moved that fast.

Saul did not stay in Gibeah. He took three thousand chosen men of Israel and went down to the Wilderness of Ziph to search for David there (1 Samuel 26:2). Saul is Israel's king, and the Ziphites are people from around Ziph who gave him the tip. Their news got him out the door fast.

David realized Saul had followed him into the wilderness, and he sent out spies to verify that Saul had arrived (1 Samuel 26:3-4). He didn't just trust a rumor. I check my oven three times before I trust it, so I respect the double-check. Careful men bake the best cookies.

This one is true. Once David realized Saul had followed him, he sent out spies to verify that Saul had arrived (1 Samuel 26:3-4). He wanted to know for sure before he made a move. Careful is a good way to be, especially with three thousand men camped nearby.

That's it, baker. Saul was lying inside the inner circle of the camp, with the troops camped around him (1 Samuel 26:5). He was in the middle, like the best cookie in the box, with everyone else tucked in around him. That's a lot of protection for one sleeping king.

Not the far edge, friend. The text says Saul was lying inside the inner circle of the camp, with the troops camped around him (1 Samuel 26:5). The troops were the ones around the outside. Saul was in the middle of them.

No back corner for this king. Saul was lying inside the inner circle of the camp, with the troops camped around him (1 Samuel 26:5). So he was at the center, with his men ringed around him. I know a thing or two about being tucked away in a back corner, and this was not that.

Right, baker. Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, answered, "I will go with you." (1 Samuel 26:6). Ahimelech the Hittite is named too, but the only answer the text writes down is Abishai's. Ahimelech's own reply isn't given.

Ahimelech the Hittite is named in the question, but he's not the one who answers. The text gives the answer of Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother: "I will go with you." (1 Samuel 26:6). Abishai is the one who stepped up and said yes.

The text only writes down one answer. Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, says, "I will go with you." (1 Samuel 26:6). Ahimelech the Hittite is named in David's question, but his reply isn't given. So Abishai is the one who walks down with David.

Yes, he did. Abishai told David, "Now, therefore, please let me thrust the spear through him into the ground with one stroke." (1 Samuel 26:8). I think Abishai saw a chance and wanted to take it. This is a heavy moment, so notice what David does next.

It's true. Abishai, Joab's brother, asked David to let him thrust the spear through Saul into the ground with one stroke (1 Samuel 26:8). He said it right over the sleeping king. It's a heavy moment, and David's answer comes next.

That's David's reason, baker. He says, "Do not destroy him, for who can extend a hand against the LORD’s anointed and be guiltless?" (1 Samuel 26:9). Saul was Israel's king, anointed by the LORD. David's reason is about the LORD, not about what might happen to him.

David doesn't mention Abner, Saul's general, in his answer. His reason is this: "…who can extend a hand against the LORD’s anointed and be guiltless?" (1 Samuel 26:9). So his reason isn't about what Abner might do. It's about who Saul is to the LORD.

Waking up isn't David's concern. He tells Abishai, "Do not destroy him, for who can extend a hand against the LORD’s anointed and be guiltless?" (1 Samuel 26:9). Nobody was waking up anyway, since a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen on them (1 Samuel 26:12). David's reason is Saul being the LORD's anointed.

That's the one. David says, "…either his day will come and he will die, or he will go into battle and perish." (1 Samuel 26:10). He leaves it in the LORD's hands. David could have taken the matter into his own, and he chose not to.

Exile isn't in David's words. He says, "…either his day will come and he will die, or he will go into battle and perish." (1 Samuel 26:10). The word is battle. David is saying the LORD will handle it, not him.

Hiding is what David was doing, but it's not what he says about Saul. His words are, "…either his day will come and he will die, or he will go into battle and perish." (1 Samuel 26:10). He is leaving Saul's end to the LORD. That's a serious thing to say standing over a sleeping king.

Half of it holds up, friend. David does stop Abishai, but he doesn't leave everything alone. He says, "…take the spear and water jug by his head, and let us go." (1 Samuel 26:11). So the spear and the water jug come along. Saul's head is left alone, and his spear and jug are not.

Right, baker. David won't let Abishai strike Saul, but he does tell him to take something. He says, "…take the spear and water jug by his head, and let us go." (1 Samuel 26:11). So the spear and water jug leave with them. That detail matters later.

explanations.answer: The LORD sent a deep sleep on them
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. No one saw them or knew about it, nor did anyone wake up, "because a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen on them." (1 Samuel 26:12). I can't keep my own kitchen quiet when one pan clangs. This was not an ordinary nap.

explanations.answer: The troops were worn out from marching
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give tiredness as the reason. It says they all remained asleep "because a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen on them." (1 Samuel 26:12). The sleep came from the LORD. That's why no one stirred.

explanations.answer: The guards were off at the far end
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about guards being away. It says they all remained asleep, "because a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen on them." (1 Samuel 26:12). The reason is the LORD's deep sleep. Everyone stayed asleep, even with two men walking through.

Not quite, friend. David shouted to the troops and to Abner son of Ner, Saul's general (1 Samuel 26:14). Abner is the one who answered, "Who are you who calls to the king?" So David's first target wasn't Saul.
That's right, baker. David shouted to the troops and to Abner son of Ner, the general of Saul's army (1 Samuel 26:14). Abner answered, "Who are you who calls to the king?" Saul only speaks up later.

explanations.answer: Why he didn’t protect the king
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. David asks, "Why then did you not protect your lord the king when one of the people came to destroy him?" (1 Samuel 26:15). Abner was the general of Saul's army, so guarding the king was on his watch. David follows it up in verse 16 by asking where the king's spear and water jug are.

explanations.answer: Why he brought so many troops
explanations.explanation: David never asks about the size of the army. His question is, "Why then did you not protect your lord the king when one of the people came to destroy him?" (1 Samuel 26:15). It's about guarding the king. Abner's job was to watch over Saul.

explanations.answer: Why he came into the wilderness
explanations.explanation: David doesn't ask Abner why he came out there. He asks, "Why then did you not protect your lord the king when one of the people came to destroy him?" (1 Samuel 26:15). So the question is about the king's safety. Abner is the general, so that was his job.

It was Saul. The text says, "Then Saul recognized David’s voice and asked, 'Is that your voice, David my son?'" (1 Samuel 26:17). That's a wide gulf and he still knew who it was. You know when someone calls your name across a parking lot and you know who it is before you even turn around? Like that.

It was Saul who recognized the voice. The text says, "Then Saul recognized David’s voice and asked, 'Is that your voice, David my son?'" (1 Samuel 26:17). David answered, "It is my voice, my lord and king." Saul knew him even across the gulf.

Yes, baker. David asks, "Why is my lord pursuing his servant? What have I done? What evil is in my hand?" (1 Samuel 26:18). He is calling Saul his lord and himself a servant. Then he asks Saul to tell him what he's done.
Rewarding isn't the word. David asks, "Why is my lord pursuing his servant?" (1 Samuel 26:18). He's talking about being chased. A reward would've made for a much nicer chat.
Summoning isn't what David says. His question is, "Why is my lord pursuing his servant?" (1 Samuel 26:18). He's asking about the chase. Summoning would just be a phone call.

That's what David says. He says men have driven him away from sharing in the inheritance of the LORD, "saying, 'Go, serve other gods.'" (1 Samuel 26:19). That's what hurts David here: being pushed away from the LORD's inheritance. I think that's why he asks about it so seriously.

explanations.answer: Go back to his father’s house
explanations.explanation: David doesn't say that. He says they have driven him away from sharing in the inheritance of the LORD, "saying, 'Go, serve other gods.'" (1 Samuel 26:19). The words are about serving other gods. They are not about going home.

Another land isn't in David's words. He says men have driven him away from sharing in the inheritance of the LORD, "saying, 'Go, serve other gods.'" (1 Samuel 26:19). So he's talking about being told to serve other gods. It's no small thing to say.

That's it, baker. David says, "…the king of Israel has come out to look for a flea, like one who hunts a partridge in the mountains." (1 Samuel 26:20). David is calling himself tiny. I know small. I once had a 25 cent price sticker on my handle.

A lion isn't what David says. He says the king has come out "to look for a flea, like one who hunts a partridge in the mountains." (1 Samuel 26:20). He's making himself sound small, not scary. A flea is about as far from a lion as you can get.

David doesn't say giant here. He says the king of Israel has come out "to look for a flea, like one who hunts a partridge in the mountains." (1 Samuel 26:20). David has met a giant before, Goliath, the Philistine champion (1 Samuel 17:4). This time he calls himself a flea.

Saul does the opposite here. He says, "I have sinned. Come back, David my son. I will never harm you again, because today you considered my life precious." (1 Samuel 26:21). He also says, "I have played the fool and have committed a grave error!" So he owns up to it.
That's right, baker. Saul says, "I have sinned. Come back, David my son." (1 Samuel 26:21). He also says, "I have played the fool and have committed a grave error!" He does admit it.

David stays right where he is. He says, "Here is the king’s spear. Let one of the young men come over and get it." (1 Samuel 26:22). He stays on his side of the gulf. Someone else has to do the walking.
That's right, friend. David stays on his side and says, "Let one of the young men come over and get it." (1 Samuel 26:22). He doesn't cross back over the gulf. A young man comes to him.

explanations.answer: To treat David’s life as precious too
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. David says, "As surely as I valued your life today, so may the LORD value my life and rescue me from all trouble." (1 Samuel 26:24). David spared Saul and now asks the LORD to value his own life the same way. It's a request for rescue.

explanations.answer: To give David the throne right away
explanations.explanation: David doesn't ask for the throne. He says, "As surely as I valued your life today, so may the LORD value my life and rescue me from all trouble." (1 Samuel 26:24). He's asking for his life to be valued and for rescue from trouble. Nothing about a crown.

explanations.answer: To punish Saul for the long chase
explanations.explanation: David doesn't ask for that. He says, "As surely as I valued your life today, so may the LORD value my life and rescue me from all trouble." (1 Samuel 26:24). He asks for his life to be valued and for rescue. Saul's punishment isn't in his words.

explanations.answer: David goes his way and Saul goes home
explanations.explanation: That's how it ends. The text says, "So David went on his way, and Saul returned home." (1 Samuel 26:25). They each head off in their own direction. No road trip together.

explanations.answer: David and Saul travel home together
explanations.explanation: They don't travel together. The text says, "So David went on his way, and Saul returned home." (1 Samuel 26:25). Saul goes home and David goes his own way. They part with the gulf still between them.

explanations.answer: David goes back into the king’s camp
explanations.explanation: David doesn't go back into the camp. The text says, "So David went on his way, and Saul returned home." (1 Samuel 26:25). He had already been in that camp once, and once was plenty. Saul is the one who goes home.
